title: This Snake Cartwheels Away From Death. #1 Actually Freezes Solid
description: This week scientists showed how a tiny Malaysian snake escapes danger by cartwheeling, about four times faster than it slithers. Just in time for Halloween, we count down five animals that cheat death, from a tail that keeps wriggling and an opossum that can't stop playing dead, to a beetle that escapes from inside a toad and a frog that freezes solid for six months.

scenes.say: Scientists just proved this tiny snake escapes danger by cartwheeling. Like a wheel.

scenes.label: This week
scenes.say: Okay, so that's real. The study came out this week, and the video looks fake. It's not.

scenes.label: Not even close
scenes.say: But here's the thing. Rolling away is not even the craziest way an animal cheats death.

scenes.label: 5 death cheaters
scenes.say: Halloween is almost here. So today, five animals that cheat death. And number one is the strangest of all.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: And stay to the very end for number one. It's an animal that basically dies every winter. Then wakes up in spring.

scenes.label: Frozen solid
scenes.say: No heartbeat. No breathing. Frozen solid for months. And we'll get to exactly how it comes back.

scenes.label: Drop the tail
scenes.say: Number five. The lizard that leaves part of itself behind on purpose.

scenes.label: Gotcha?
scenes.say: Picture a fox pouncing on a lizard. It grabs the tail. Game over, right? Nope.

scenes.label: Snap
scenes.say: Many lizards can drop their tail. Some do it by squeezing muscles at the base until the tail snaps off. And here's the creepy part. The tail keeps wriggling on its own, for up to about five minutes.

scenes.label: Wrong target
scenes.say: So the fox is staring at this thrashing tail, while the actual lizard is long gone.

scenes.label: A body decoy
scenes.say: Think about that. The lizard's escape plan is literally a decoy made out of its own body.

scenes.label: 4 minutes of chaos
scenes.say: One alligator lizard tail was seen thrashing for roughly four minutes before it finally stopped.

scenes.label: Cartilage, not bone
scenes.say: Does it grow back? Kind of. The new tail is usually shorter, and it's made of cartilage instead of bone.

scenes.label: Two tails?
scenes.say: And sometimes two tails grow back from one break. Yes, a lizard with a forked tail.

scenes.label: The price
scenes.say: And it's not free. The tail stores fat, so losing it means losing an energy reserve. But being alive beats being lunch.

scenes.label: Last resort
scenes.say: Losing it can also slow a lizard down and mess with its balance when it climbs. So it's a last resort.

scenes.label: Next level
scenes.say: Okay, but dropping a tail is easy. What if your whole body has to look dead?

scenes.label: Playing possum
scenes.say: Number four. The animal that plays dead so well, it can't even stop.

scenes.label: Cornered
scenes.say: A coyote corners an opossum. And suddenly the opossum just falls over.

scenes.label: Looks dead
scenes.say: It rolls on its side, goes stiff, and stares blankly. Its teeth are bared, and it drools foam. Its breathing slows. You can nudge it, even pick it up, and it won't fight back.

scenes.label: The smell
scenes.say: Then it releases a foul-smelling fluid from glands under its tail. It smells like something that's been dead for a while.

scenes.label: No thanks
scenes.say: Lots of predators don't want to eat something that already looks and smells rotten. So they walk away.

scenes.label: Not an act
scenes.say: Now here's the twist. The San Diego Zoo says it's not really an act. It's involuntary, more like fainting.

scenes.label: Up to 4 hours
scenes.say: And that state can last up to four hours. Four hours lying there, while a predator gives up and leaves.

scenes.label: Would you wait?
scenes.say: Now, quick question for you. If you were the coyote, would you wait four hours? Most predators don't. Fun extra fact. Opossums have about fifty teeth. More than any other land mammal in North America.

scenes.label: Or just run?
scenes.say: Okay, so lizards drop body parts, opossums fake death. But what if you could just leave? Fast.

scenes.label: The rolling snake
scenes.say: Number three. Back to the snake from the start, the one that cartwheels.

scenes.label: Malaysia
scenes.say: It lives in the rainforest of Kubah National Park in Malaysia. It's called a dwarf reed snake.

scenes.label: Max 9 inches
scenes.say: And it's tiny. Dwarf reed snakes grow to nine inches at most. Smaller than a ruler.

scenes.label: Filmed in 2019
scenes.say: Back in 2019, researchers filmed one doing something no one had formally recorded in any snake. It rolled.

scenes.label: A world first
scenes.say: A 2023 paper called it the first formal observation of cartwheeling in any snake. Or any reptile at all.

scenes.label: 13 snakes tested
scenes.say: So the team went back and tested 13 of these little snakes to see how they do it.

scenes.label: Current Biology
scenes.say: This week, in the journal Current Biology, the team led by Yosuke Kojima of Toho University showed how it works.

scenes.label: Curl and roll
scenes.say: The snake curls into a tight loop, head up. Then it rolls forward like a wheel.

scenes.label: Airborne
scenes.say: It pushes off with its tail and is briefly in the air. It twists, lands on one side, and rolls again. And the whole time, it keeps its head fairly steady. Researchers think that might help it keep its bearings.

scenes.label: Up to 8 mph
scenes.say: And it's fast. The rolling snakes hit about four to eight miles an hour. That's roughly four times faster than their normal slithering. For a nine-inch snake, that's a getaway car.

scenes.label: Relatives can't
scenes.say: They also tested close relatives, other reed snakes. Not one of them rolled.

scenes.label: Still a mystery
scenes.say: Why do they do it? Honestly, scientists don't know yet. Or how long they can keep it up.

scenes.label: Could others roll?
scenes.say: Jessica Tingle at Brown University, who wasn't part of the study, asked a fun question. Do other snakes have the right body for this, but just never try?

scenes.label: Already eaten?
scenes.say: But what if the predator already caught you? What if you're already swallowed?

scenes.label: Bombardier beetle
scenes.say: Number two. The bug that escapes from inside a stomach.

scenes.label: Its weapon
scenes.say: Meet the bombardier beetle. Its weapon is a chemical blast it shoots from its rear end.

scenes.label: 649 species
scenes.say: And there are a lot of them. Scientists count 649 species of bombardier beetles.

scenes.label: About 100°C
scenes.say: Researchers at MIT found the spray comes out at about 100 degrees Celsius. That's boiling water.

scenes.label: Up to 735 a second
scenes.say: And it doesn't fire once. It fires in rapid pulses, between about 368 and 735 a second.

scenes.label: One gulp
scenes.say: Now, toads swallow bugs whole. In one gulp. So what happens when a toad swallows this one?

scenes.label: Kobe University
scenes.say: Scientists at Kobe University in Japan tested exactly that, with Asian bombardier beetles and Japanese toads.

scenes.label: Toad says no
scenes.say: Inside the toad, the beetle keeps firing its boiling spray. And often, the toad throws it back up.

scenes.label: 43% escaped
scenes.say: In the study, about 43 percent of beetles that could still spray got vomited out. Every single one of those was alive.

scenes.label: 35% vs 57%
scenes.say: Here's a weird detail. Toads from the beetle's own habitat threw it up 35 percent of the time. Toads from elsewhere, 57 percent.

scenes.label: 107 minutes
scenes.say: Some were thrown up after 12 minutes. One beetle was inside a toad for 107 minutes, and still came out alive.

scenes.label: No spray, no escape
scenes.say: Beetles whose spray had been used up first? All of them got digested.

scenes.label: Not all made it
scenes.say: To be fair, it's not a perfect happy ending. Of the beetles thrown up, one survived at least two more weeks.

scenes.label: Ready for #1?
scenes.say: But number one doesn't escape death. It goes all the way there, and comes back.

scenes.label: Wood frog
scenes.say: Number one. The frog that freezes solid every winter.

scenes.label: Alaska
scenes.say: This is the wood frog, and some of them live near Fairbanks, Alaska. Brutal winters.

scenes.label: Lets itself freeze
scenes.say: Instead of escaping the cold, it hides in leaf litter on the ground and just lets itself freeze.

scenes.label: Heart stops
scenes.say: Up to 60 percent of its body freezes. Its heart stops. Its breathing stops.

scenes.label: Looks dead
scenes.say: If you found one, you'd say it's dead. Honestly, by most definitions, it looks dead.

scenes.label: In the wild
scenes.say: Researchers from the University of Alaska Fairbanks tracked frogs freezing in the wild. Not in a lab. Outside.

scenes.label: Minus 18°C
scenes.say: Those frogs survived temperatures down to about minus 18 degrees Celsius. That's around zero Fahrenheit.

scenes.label: Maybe colder
scenes.say: And the scientists think that's not even the limit. They suspect wood frogs could handle around minus 20.

scenes.label: 193 days frozen
scenes.say: And they stayed frozen for about 193 days on average. More than six months of not being alive, sort of.

scenes.label: 100% survived
scenes.say: Every one of those wild frogs survived. In earlier lab tests, frogs only handled about two months.

scenes.label: Sugar shield
scenes.say: So how? Here's the secret. The frog floods its organs with sugar. The heart gets loaded with glucose.

scenes.label: 10x more sugar
scenes.say: Wild frogs had roughly ten times more sugar in their hearts than frogs frozen in the lab. That sugar works like antifreeze inside its cells, so the ice doesn't tear them apart.

scenes.label: 10 to 15 rehearsals
scenes.say: Before the deep freeze, wild frogs go through about 10 to 15 freeze-thaw cycles. Scientists think that's what builds up all that sugar.

scenes.label: Back in spring
scenes.say: Then spring comes. It thaws out, the heart starts beating again, and it hops off like nothing happened.

scenes.label: Real zombie
scenes.say: So forget zombies this Halloween. The real thing is a frog in Alaska.

scenes.label: Your pick?
scenes.say: Okay, which one surprised you most? The rolling snake, the beetle, or the frozen frog? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: This Frog's Heart Stops Every Winter. Why Is It Alive?
short.description: Wood frogs in Alaska let up to 60% of their body freeze, survive about −18°C and stay frozen ~193 days, then thaw and hop away in spring. Sources: Larson et al. 2014 (J. Exp. Biol.), Audubon.

scenes.say: This frog's heart stops every winter. And it isn't dead.
Wood frogs in Alaska hide in the leaves and let up to 60 percent of their body freeze solid.
No heartbeat. No breathing. Scientists tracked wild ones surviving about minus 18 degrees Celsius.
And they stayed frozen for about 193 days. That's over six months. Every single one survived.
In the lab, frogs only lasted about two months. Out in the wild, they lasted three times longer.
The trick? It floods its organs with sugar, a natural antifreeze, so ice can't wreck its cells.
Then spring comes, it thaws, and the heart starts beating again like nothing happened.
So next time you see a frozen frog, remember. This frog's heart stops every winter.
